songs.title: Let It Be
songs.why: Slow, clear, every word audible. Paul McCartney wrote it after a dream about his mother.

focus.m: accept a situation and stop fighting it

songs.ask: Who gives the advice in this song, and when does she come?

songs.title: Here Comes the Sun
songs.why: Written in a garden on the first warm day after a long winter. Listen for the relief.

focus.m: here comes + noun: announcing an arrival (here comes the bus)

songs.ask: What season is ending, and what is happening to the ice?

songs.title: Imagine
songs.why: One idea per line in the simplest English possible. That simplicity is a skill.

focus.m: imagine + -ing / imagine there is…: picture a situation in your mind

songs.ask: Count the things he asks you to imagine the world without.

songs.title: Every Breath You Take
songs.why: Played at weddings for forty years. Listen twice and decide whether it is a love song at all.

focus.m: take a breath, make a move, take a step: verb + noun pairs

songs.ask: Is the singer loving or watching? Which words told you?

songs.title: Don't Speak
songs.why: A break-up song sung by the person being left. The voice does half the grammar for you.

focus.m: a negative imperative; compare 'say nothing' and 'be quiet'

songs.ask: Why does she not want to hear the explanation?

songs.title: Wish You Were Here
songs.why: About a friend who disappeared into himself. The guitar at the start sounds like a radio in another room.

focus.m: wish + past simple for a wish about the present

songs.ask: The song asks you to tell two opposite things apart. Which pairs?

songs.title: Time
songs.why: The clocks at the start were recorded one by one in a shop. The lyric is about a wasted decade.

focus.m: kill time, run out of time, in no time, time flies: four phrases to collect

songs.ask: What was the singer doing while the years went by?

songs.title: Under Pressure
songs.why: Two singers who did not plan to meet, one famous bass line, a lyric that turns from fear to love.

focus.m: be / come / put someone under pressure

songs.ask: What does the song say pressure does to ordinary people?

songs.title: Blowin' in the Wind
songs.why: A song made almost entirely of questions, and one refusal to answer them.

focus.m: how many + plural noun; how much + uncountable

songs.ask: How many questions does he ask before the first answer?

songs.title: The Sound of Silence
songs.why: Two voices so close they sound like one. It is about people who talk and never say anything.

focus.m: a paradox: two opposite ideas joined on purpose

songs.ask: What are the people in the crowd doing wrong?

songs.title: Bridge Over Troubled Water
songs.why: A promise to a friend, sung by Art Garfunkel alone. Gospel pace, dictionary-clear diction.

focus.m: troubled = full of problems; also 'troubled times', 'a troubled look'

songs.ask: List the situations in which the singer promises to help.

songs.title: What a Wonderful World
songs.why: A list of ordinary things, sung by a man who had seen plenty of the other kind.

focus.m: what + a + adjective + noun: an exclamation (what a day)

songs.ask: Which colours does he name, and what has each one?

songs.title: Can't Help Falling in Love
songs.why: Based on an eighteenth-century French melody. Three minutes of soft consonants.

focus.m: cannot stop yourself doing something

songs.ask: Who rushes in, according to the opening line?

songs.title: My Way
songs.why: A man looking back at his whole life in the past simple and present perfect. Listen for both tenses.

focus.m: do it my way = in the way I choose; also 'have it your way'

songs.ask: Which things does he say he has had 'a few' of?

songs.title: Hotel California
songs.why: A story song: a traveller, a hotel, a door that will not open. Follow it like a short film.

focus.m: check out of a hotel; check something out = look at it

songs.ask: What can the guest do, and what can he never do?

songs.title: Dreams
songs.why: Written in ten minutes during a band break-up, about the band break-up.

focus.m: have a dream, follow a dream, a dream come true

songs.ask: What does the singer say happens only when it rains?

songs.title: Three Little Birds
songs.why: The easiest reggae song to understand, and the most repeated advice in pop music.

focus.m: worry about + noun / -ing; 'no worries' in casual speech

songs.ask: Where are the birds, and what is their message?

songs.title: Redemption Song
songs.why: Just a voice and an acoustic guitar. Written when he was already ill, about freeing the mind.

focus.m: being saved from a bad past; redeem yourself

songs.ask: What kind of slavery does he ask people to free themselves from?

songs.title: Wonderwall
songs.why: The song every guitarist learns first. Mancunian vowels: good practice for real British accents.

focus.m: by now = at this point in time (you should have realised by now)

songs.ask: What does the singer hope the other person will be for him?

songs.title: Don't Look Back in Anger
songs.why: A stadium sing-along with a gentle piece of advice in the title.

focus.m: look back = think about the past; in anger = angrily

songs.ask: Who is Sally, and what should she not do?

songs.title: Creep
songs.why: A song about not fitting in, sung quietly then very loudly. The verses are almost spoken.

focus.m: belong here / belong to someone / a sense of belonging

songs.ask: Which two words does he use to describe himself in the chorus?

songs.title: Fix You
songs.why: Written for a grieving friend. The first half is a hymn, the second half is a march.

focus.m: fix a problem, fix a time, fix someone (repair, in a kind sense)

songs.ask: Make a list of the 'when you…' situations in the first verse.

songs.title: The Scientist
songs.why: The video runs backwards; the singer had to learn the words in reverse. Listen for apologies.

focus.m: start again from the beginning

songs.ask: What does he say nobody told him?

songs.title: Someone Like You
songs.why: One voice, one piano, and a conversation with an ex. Every second line is a complete sentence.

focus.m: it does not matter; forget it

songs.ask: What has the other person done since they parted?

songs.title: Shape of My Heart
songs.why: A gambler who plays not for money but to understand something. Card vocabulary throughout.

focus.m: deal the cards; a deal; deal with a problem

songs.ask: Why does the gambler play, if not for the money?

songs.title: Englishman in New York
songs.why: About being foreign and staying yourself. The line about manners is worth memorising.

focus.m: alien = a foreigner (formal, in law); also a being from space

songs.ask: List the small habits that mark the singer as English.

songs.title: Brothers in Arms
songs.why: A soldier's last words to his comrades. Slow, every consonant clear, a guitar instead of a chorus.

focus.m: fellow soldiers; people who fought together

songs.ask: Where does the soldier say he was born, and where will he die?

songs.title: Losing My Religion
songs.why: The title is a Southern American idiom, not about religion at all. A mandolin carries the whole song.

focus.m: US South idiom: lose your patience or temper

songs.ask: Where is the singer standing, and what does he say he has done too much of?

songs.title: With or Without You
songs.why: Four chords for five minutes and it never gets boring. A lesson in building tension.

focus.m: a fixed pair; also 'sooner or later', 'more or less'

songs.ask: Which things does he say he cannot do?

songs.title: Come As You Are
songs.why: Three words of welcome in the title, then a verse full of contradictions on purpose.

focus.m: come without changing or dressing up

songs.ask: Find two instructions in the lyric that cancel each other out.

songs.title: Fast Car
songs.why: A whole life in four minutes: leaving, working, hoping, repeating. Story told in plain past tense.

focus.m: agree an arrangement; also 'a big deal', 'no big deal'

songs.ask: What is the deal the singer suggests at the start?

songs.title: Hallelujah
songs.why: Eighty verses were written; four survive. Even the sad lines keep a straight face.

focus.m: a Hebrew word of praise; in English speech, relief ('finally, hallelujah')

songs.ask: What two kinds of hallelujah does the song describe?

songs.title: Dreams
songs.why: An Irish voice that slides between notes. The lyric is about change arriving from every direction.

focus.m: in every way; possible adds emphasis

songs.ask: What is changing, and how often?

songs.title: Father and Son
songs.why: Two voices in one singer: the father low and slow, the son higher and quicker.

focus.m: start a calm, stable life; also 'calm down'

songs.ask: What does the father advise, and what does the son answer?

songs.title: Stand by Me
songs.why: A bass line you will recognise in two seconds and a promise in three words.

focus.m: support someone in a hard time

songs.ask: Which frightening things does he say he will not fear?

songs.title: Piano Man
songs.why: A bar on a Saturday night, one character per verse. A gallery of small portraits.

focus.m: feel like having or doing something

songs.ask: Name three people in the bar and what each one does.

songs.title: Yesterday
songs.why: The most covered song ever written. Past tense all the way through, until one 'now'.

focus.m: yesterday, the day before, the other day: three ways to point backwards

songs.ask: What has changed between yesterday and today for the singer?

songs.title: Your Song
songs.why: A song about writing a song, with the hesitations left in. Listen for the spoken-style asides.

focus.m: a polite way to introduce something you did

songs.ask: Which gifts does he say he could not afford?

songs.title: Lean on Me
songs.why: A gospel hand-clap and an offer of help. The whole lyric is advice you could use.

focus.m: depend on someone for support

songs.ask: What does the song say we all need, and what should we swallow?

songs.title: Feeling Good
songs.why: A new day described thing by thing. Brass arrives like sunrise halfway through.

focus.m: feel good / feel well / feel like: three different meanings

songs.ask: Which creatures and things does she say know how she feels?

words.m: a small difference in meaning, tone or feeling
words.ex: Her answer showed real nuance: she agreed, but with conditions.
words.say: Describe a nuance in your own language that English lacks.

words.m: able to recover quickly from difficulty
words.ex: Children are often more resilient than adults expect.
words.say: Who is the most resilient person you know, and why?

words.m: very careful about every detail
words.ex: He kept meticulous notes on every lesson.
words.say: What is one task you are meticulous about?

words.m: seeming to be everywhere
words.ex: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in classrooms.
words.say: Name something ubiquitous today that did not exist when you were a child.

words.m: having mixed feelings about something
words.ex: I am ambivalent about living abroad: tempting, but far from family.
words.say: What are you ambivalent about at the moment?

words.m: so strong or interesting that it holds attention or convinces
words.ex: The documentary made a compelling case for cycling lanes.
words.say: Give a compelling reason to learn a third language.

words.m: harmful
words.ex: Late nights are detrimental to memory.
words.say: Name a habit that is detrimental to studying.

words.m: possible and practical to do
words.ex: Is it feasible to finish the essay in forty minutes?
words.say: Is a car-free city centre feasible where you live?

words.m: certain to happen; unavoidable
words.ex: Some mistakes are inevitable when you speak fast.
words.say: What change in your city seems inevitable?

words.m: very great or deep (of an effect, feeling or idea)
words.ex: The book had a profound effect on how I plan my days.
words.say: What has had a profound effect on your English?

words.m: to examine something very carefully
words.ex: Examiners scrutinise the second paragraph more than you think.
words.say: What should governments scrutinise more closely?

words.m: not obvious; delicate and hard to notice
words.ex: There is a subtle difference between 'fun' and 'funny'.
words.say: Describe a subtle difference between two words you confuse.

words.m: to grow or develop well; to flourish
words.ex: Small shops thrive when parking is easy.
words.say: In what conditions do you thrive?

words.m: of little importance
words.ex: Spelling may seem trivial, but it costs marks.
words.say: What do people argue about that is actually trivial?

words.m: able to do many different things well
words.ex: English is a versatile word: it can be a noun or an adjective.
words.say: Name a versatile person or tool in your life.

words.m: to make a problem or pain less severe
words.ex: A short walk alleviates the tiredness of a long lesson.
words.say: How could a city alleviate traffic?

words.m: logical and well organised; easy to follow
words.ex: A coherent essay moves in one direction.
words.say: What makes a speaker sound coherent?

words.m: to become worse
words.ex: Air quality deteriorates in winter.
words.say: What has deteriorated in your town in the last ten years?

words.m: to improve the quality or value of something
words.ex: Reading aloud enhances pronunciation.
words.say: What enhances a city for young people?

words.m: to make a bad situation worse
words.ex: Cheap cars exacerbate congestion.
words.say: What exacerbates stress before an exam?

words.m: to make progress difficult
words.ex: Fear of mistakes hinders fluency.
words.say: What hinders people from learning languages?

words.m: to put a plan or decision into action
words.ex: The school implemented a no-phone rule.
words.say: What rule would you implement at your school?

words.m: to reduce the harm or seriousness of something
words.ex: Trees mitigate the heat of summer streets.
words.say: How can a family mitigate its impact on the environment?

words.m: an idea or belief
words.ex: The notion that talent is fixed does a lot of damage.
words.say: What common notion about learning do you disagree with?

words.m: more important than anything else
words.ex: In Part 2, keeping talking is paramount.
words.say: What is paramount when choosing a job?

words.m: dealing with things practically rather than by theory
words.ex: A pragmatic learner records herself instead of reading about accents.
words.say: Are you more pragmatic or more idealistic?

words.m: common, widespread at a particular time or place
words.ex: Online lessons are now prevalent in cities.
words.say: What habit is prevalent among your friends?

words.m: unwilling and hesitant
words.ex: Many students are reluctant to speak first.
words.say: What are you reluctant to do, but do anyway?

words.m: to keep something going over time
words.ex: It is hard to sustain motivation for a year.
words.say: How do you sustain a good habit?

words.m: real and able to be seen, touched or measured
words.ex: A band score is tangible; confidence is not.
words.say: What tangible result do you want by December?

words.m: to support or form the basis of something
words.ex: Vocabulary underpins every IELTS skill.
words.say: What underpins a good friendship?

words.m: easily harmed, physically or emotionally
words.ex: Older people are vulnerable to heat.
words.say: Which group in society is most vulnerable, and why?

words.m: without hope or comfort; cold and empty
words.ex: The report paints a bleak picture of city air.
words.say: Describe a bleak place you have seen.

words.m: honest and direct, even when it is uncomfortable
words.ex: Her candid feedback saved me a month.
words.say: When is it better not to be candid?

words.m: frightening because it seems difficult
words.ex: A 250-word essay looks daunting until you plan it.
words.say: What is the most daunting thing about speaking English?

words.m: to add more detail or explanation
words.ex: Examiners want you to elaborate, not just answer.
words.say: Answer a question, then elaborate for thirty seconds.

words.m: lasting only a short time
words.ex: A fleeting moment of panic before the recording starts.
words.say: Describe a fleeting moment you remember well.

words.m: real, sincere; not fake
words.ex: A genuine question gets a longer answer.
words.say: What is one genuine interest of yours outside study?

words.m: very busy and full of activity
words.ex: Exam week is hectic for teachers too.
words.say: Describe your most hectic day of the week.

words.m: to involve yourself completely in something
words.ex: Immerse yourself: films, songs, labels on tins.
words.say: How do you immerse yourself in English at home?

words.m: to put something at risk
words.ex: One late night can jeopardise a week of sleep.
words.say: What could jeopardise your target score?

words.m: eager, enthusiastic
words.ex: She is keen on films and keen to discuss them.
words.say: What are you keen to try next year?

words.m: clear and easy to understand
words.ex: A lucid answer uses short sentences.
words.say: Who explains things most lucidly in your life?

words.m: ordinary and dull
words.ex: Even mundane tasks become practice if you narrate them in English.
words.say: Describe a mundane routine in interesting words.

words.m: so small that it does not matter
words.ex: The cost of a second-hand book is negligible.
words.say: What has a negligible effect that people think is important?

words.m: to be greater or more important than
words.ex: The benefits of early sleep outweigh the lost hour.
words.say: Do the advantages of city life outweigh the disadvantages?

words.m: seeming reasonable or likely to be true
words.ex: It is a plausible excuse, but still an excuse.
words.say: Give a plausible reason why people read less.

words.m: attractively old-fashioned or unusual
words.ex: The old quarter is quaint, with tiny bakeries.
words.say: Describe a quaint place near your home.

words.m: strong and unlikely to fail
words.ex: A robust routine survives a bad week.
words.say: What makes a study routine robust?

words.m: not easily convinced; having doubts
words.ex: I am sceptical of apps that promise fluency in a month.
words.say: What claim are you sceptical about?

words.m: too long, slow and boring
words.ex: Copying word lists is tedious; using them is not.
words.say: What tedious task would you automate?

words.m: never done or known before
words.ex: The city grew at an unprecedented rate.
words.say: Name an unprecedented change in your lifetime.

words.m: producing clear, strong images in the mind
words.ex: A vivid example beats three general sentences.
words.say: Describe a vivid memory from childhood.

words.m: very tired, often after a long effort
words.ex: By the third passage most candidates are weary.
words.say: What are you weary of hearing people say?

words.m: to want something very much, with longing
words.ex: In winter everyone yearns for the first warm day.
words.say: What do you yearn for when you are abroad?

words.m: to control or limit something
words.ex: Cities curb car use with high parking fees.
words.say: How can parents curb screen time without a fight?

words.m: to keep thinking or talking about something, especially something bad
words.ex: Do not dwell on one wrong answer during the test.
words.say: What do people dwell on too much?

words.m: to fail to appreciate something because it is always there
words.ex: We take clean water for granted until it stops.
words.say: What do you take for granted that others do not have?

words.m: looking back at the past with the knowledge you have now
words.ex: In hindsight, I should have started Anki in March.
words.say: What would you do differently, in hindsight?

words.m: causing loss or harm to something else
words.ex: Speed at the expense of accuracy costs marks.
words.say: What do people gain at the expense of their health?

films.title: Dead Poets Society
films.why: A teacher who makes boys stand on desks to see the room differently. Slow, warm, full of poetry read aloud.

listen.m: the English for the Latin motto at the heart of the film: make the most of today

films.ask: Should teachers break rules to inspire students? Where is the line?

films.title: Good Will Hunting
films.why: A janitor who is a genius, a therapist who will not give up. Boston accents and long, honest conversations.

listen.m: fault = responsibility for a mistake; compare 'to blame'

films.ask: Is talent wasted if a person chooses an ordinary life?

films.title: The Truman Show
films.why: A man whose whole life is a television programme, and he does not know. Funny first, then not.

listen.p: in case I don't see you
listen.m: in case = because something might happen

films.ask: Would you leave a comfortable world that is fake for a real one that is hard?

films.title: Forrest Gump
films.why: Thirty years of American history told by a man who keeps running. Simple sentences, big feelings.

listen.m: a simile: as unpredictable as… ; collect 'like a' comparisons

films.ask: Is a simple life a happy life? Use Forrest as an example.

films.title: The Shawshank Redemption
films.why: Twenty years in prison, patience, and a friendship. The narration is the clearest English in cinema.

listen.m: get busy + -ing: start doing something with energy

films.ask: Why do people say hope is dangerous? Do you agree?

films.title: The King's Speech
films.why: A king who stammers and the speech teacher who treats him as an equal. A film about pronunciation.

listen.m: become able to express yourself; also literal, here

films.ask: How much does confidence matter compared with accuracy when speaking?

films.title: About Time
films.why: A man who can relive any day, and learns to live each one once. British English, gentle pace.

listen.m: get the maximum benefit or pleasure from something

films.ask: If you could repeat one day, would it make you happier or less present?

films.title: Groundhog Day
films.why: The same day, again and again, until a cynical man gets it right. The title became an English idiom.

listen.m: now an idiom: a situation that repeats itself tediously

films.ask: What would you learn if you had unlimited time and no consequences?

films.title: The Intern
films.why: A seventy-year-old intern at a fashion start-up. Office English, polite and modern.

listen.m: get old = become boring or stale (and the pun on age)

films.ask: What can older and younger colleagues learn from each other?

films.title: Whiplash
films.why: A drummer and a teacher who pushes too far. Loud, fast, and a question about how we get good.

listen.m: not quite = almost but not exactly; a soft British-style no

films.ask: Does pressure make people better, or just afraid?

films.title: The Pursuit of Happyness
films.why: A father and son with nowhere to sleep, and an unpaid internship. Based on a true story.

listen.m: pursuit = the effort to achieve something; pursue a career

films.ask: Is money a condition for happiness? Where does the film stand?

films.title: Before Sunrise
films.why: Two strangers walk around Vienna for one night and talk. Nothing happens; everything happens.

listen.m: gradually become familiar with a person or place

films.ask: Can you really know someone in one conversation?

films.title: The Terminal
films.why: A man trapped in an airport learns English from television and kindness. Watch how he does it.

listen.m: while waiting for something else to happen

films.ask: What is the best way to learn a language without a classroom?

films.title: Notting Hill
films.why: A bookshop owner and a film star. London English at its most polite and most awkward.

listen.m: 'just a' softens or makes something smaller: just a girl, just a thought

films.ask: Does fame make an ordinary life impossible?

films.title: Up
films.why: The first ten minutes tell a whole marriage without words. Then a house flies.

listen.m: out there = in the wider world, waiting

films.ask: What makes an ordinary life an adventure?

films.title: Paddington 2
films.why: A polite bear in London and a village of good manners. The best British English for learners.

listen.m: a first conditional used as a rule for life

films.ask: Is politeness a strength or a weakness in a big city?

films.title: Inside Out
films.why: Five emotions inside one girl's head. The vocabulary of feelings, made visible.

listen.m: core = central, most important; also core skills, core values

films.ask: Is sadness useful? What does the film argue?

films.title: 12 Angry Men
films.why: One room, twelve men, one decision. The whole film is an argument, and it is black and white.

listen.m: a legal standard: enough doubt that a sensible person would hesitate

films.ask: Can one person change the mind of a group? How?
